newsitem.title: UK: POLL - Dollar to drop over next twelve months.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Dollar to drop over next twelve months.

text.p: The dollar is expected to fall against the mark and the yen over the next 12 months as central banks rebuff attempts to drive the U.S. currency higher, a Reuters survey of currency strategists across the world showed.

In the survey of 55 contributors, the median forecast showed the dollar at 1.88 marks and 118 yen at the end of this month. By end-July 1998, the dollar is expected to drop to 1.7550 marks and 110 yen.
The dollar closed at 1.8795 marks and 119.20 yen on August 5, the final day of the survey.
Peter Luxton, director of global currency at Standard & Poors' MMS in London, said he expected the central banks of Germany, Japan and the United States to use intervention to push the dollar down.

"The Bundebank is keeping quiet, but mark weakness risks importing inflation into Germany. They may be trying to catch the market out, long and wrong," Luxton said. "Levels above 120 yen are sensitive to U.S. criticism because of on-going trade friction."
In an effort to redress the huge bilateral trade imbalance, the U.S. and Japanese authorities allowed the dollar to fall to a post World War II low of 79.70 yen on April 30, 1995.
Inflation imported because of the weak mark, and signs that the German economy may be coming back to life mean the Bundesbank will start thinking about higher interest rates, analysts said.
The German central bank fixed the repo at an unchanged three percent in mid-July for two weeks only ahead of its four-week recess.
This has prompted speculation that the bank might opt for a variable repo rate tender in the second half of its summer break.

"There is the possibility of a dual repo, half fixed and half variable. If this happens the markets will expect higher interest rates," said Nick Shamin, currency strategist at ANZ Investment Bank in London.
Andrea Zuccheri, currency strategist at Sella Asset Management in Milan, believes the dollar will stabilise against the mark at current levels.
"It is unlikely the Bundesbank will allow the mark to fall much further. Neither do we believe the Bundesbank will nudge interest rates higher," Zuccheri said.
"The dollar will remain strong until the new European single currency...comes into being. The uncertainty will disappear once the conversion rates are decided."
Expectations that European economic and monetary union (EMU) will go ahead on time in January 1999 with a broad membership, has been the major factor behind mark weakness.
The expected inclusion in the euro of historically volatile currencies such as the Italian lira has prompted many investors to move into dollar assets.
The lowest one-month prediction in the poll for the dollar was 1.7700 marks, and the highest was 1.9250 marks.
Analysts who see the dollar continuing to move higher say good economic growth and subdued inflationary pressures in the United States are the main reason.

"The U.S. economy is in good shape and there is a dissatisfaction with everything European. The dollar will be bought against everything for the rest of this year," said Alan Collins, head of technical analysis at Merita Bank in London.
The one-month forecast range for the dollar versus the yen was 114 to 122.
The continuing weakness in the Japanese economy and the prospect of no change in monetary policy means that the interest rate differential will remain in favour of the dollar, analysts said.
With the Federal funds rate at 5.5 percent and the Japanese discount rate at 0.5 percent, the carry costs of a short dollar position are too high, they said.
